summary: Existing RFCs let multicast traffic cross sites within one BGP/MPLS VPN. This standards-track RFC specifies procedures for an MVPN extranet, where multicast from a source in one VPN reaches receivers in another. It updates RFCs 6513, 6514 and 6625.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC lets a multicast source in one VPN reach receivers in a different VPN over the same provider network. It works by importing a chosen set of routes between the two VPNs and adding rules so that traffic is delivered to the right place and never to the wrong one.

subtitle: How a multicast source in one VPN reaches receivers in another VPN over the same provider network.

tldr.problem: Multicast VPN procedures let a multicast flow travel between sites of one VPN, but many customers need a source in one VPN to reach receivers in a different VPN, and the earlier procedures do not cover that case.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds procedures for building an extranet: import a selected set of routes between the two VPNs, use Route Targets to keep the imports apart, pick one of two transmission models, and make sure a receiver can tell which tunnel a flow should have arrived on.
tldr.outcome: Extranet MVPN service becomes possible for PIM-SM customers using either PIM or BGP between provider routers. The RFC updates RFC 6513, RFC 6514 and RFC 6625, and is itself updated by RFC 8534.

facts.label: Transmission models
facts.value: Single PMSI per C-flow; multiple PMSIs per C-flow

facts.label: Route distinguishers with separation
facts.value: One default RD and one extranet RD

today: RFC 7900 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2016. It updates RFC 6513, RFC 6514 and RFC 6625, and is itself updated by RFC 8534. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What an MVPN Extranet Is
sections.content:
Earlier RFCs, RFC 6513 and RFC 6514, describe how IP multicast traffic travels from one site to another inside a single BGP/MPLS IP VPN. This RFC covers the case where a multicast source sits in one VPN and the receivers sit in another, which is called an MVPN extranet. It adds the procedures needed on top of the earlier ones and updates RFCs 6513, 6514 and RFC 6625.

The basic setup is two VPNs. VPN-S holds the extranet sources, each in its own VRF, and VPN-R holds the receivers. Every VRF has an import and an export Route Target, so a receiver in VPN-R normally cannot see anything from VPN-S. Building an extranet means exporting a selected set of routes from the VPN-S VRFs and importing them into the VPN-R VRFs, and then making sure the multicast data actually travels the right way between them.

The customers set the policy and the service provider implements it by provisioning the import and export Route Targets of the VRFs. The document assumes that customer sites run PIM-SM, and it covers both the ASM and the SSM service models.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC lets a multicast source in one VPN reach receivers in a different VPN, over the same provider network. It works by importing a chosen set of routes between the two VPNs and adding rules so the traffic is not delivered to the wrong place.

sections.title: The Vocabulary of Extranet Multicast
sections.content:
The RFC borrows the C- and P- prefixes of RFC 6513, where a C-thing belongs to the customer and a P-thing to the provider. An extranet C-source is a source that policy allows to send to receivers in other VPNs. An extranet C-receiver is a receiver that policy allows to receive from sources in other VPNs. An extranet C-flow is the multicast flow made of one such source and one group, and an extranet C-group is a group address in the Any-Source Multicast range that has extranet sources and receivers. The extranet C-RP is the Rendezvous Point for such a group, allowed to accept PIM Register messages from outside its own VPN and to send data to extranet receivers outside its VPN.

A P-tunnel is the provider's tunnel that carries the multicast data across the backbone, and it is identified by the PMSI Tunnel attribute of the BGP auto-discovery route that advertises it. The RFC also defines a VPN security violation as any situation in which a packet is delivered to a VPN even though policy says it should not be delivered there.
sections.plainLanguage: The document uses C- for customer addresses and P- for provider ones. An extranet source is a source allowed to send outside its own VPN, and an extranet receiver is a receiver allowed to listen to sources from other VPNs.

sections.title: Extranet Transmission Models
sections.content:
A VRF that holds extranet sources or receivers must use exactly one of the RFC's transmission models, and the source VRF and the receiver VRF must use the same one. The choice is made by provisioning.

In the single PMSI per C-flow model, a provider edge router transmits each packet of an extranet flow on only one PMSI, so the flow travels on one P-tunnel. This model has two variants. Without extranet separation, traffic from extranet sources and from ordinary sources may share a P-tunnel. With extranet separation, the two kinds of traffic must never share a P-tunnel, which reduces the traffic delivered unnecessarily and removes one of the ambiguity problems described later.

In the multiple PMSIs per C-flow model, a provider edge router may send the packets of an extranet flow on several PMSIs. The RFC gives procedures for this model when PIM is the provider-to-provider control protocol. Support for extranet separation with PIM is out of scope, as is support for the multiple-PMSI model when BGP is the control protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: One model sends each extranet flow over a single provider tunnel. The other lets a flow use several tunnels. The source VPN and the receiver VPN must pick the same model, and the choice is made when the service is set up.

sections.title: Distributing the Routes That Match Source Addresses
sections.content:
For a flow to cross the provider backbone, the receiver VRF must import a route that matches the source address and that is eligible for Upstream Multicast Hop selection. Such a route does not have to be a unicast route: SAFI 129 routes can be used instead, which lets the flow be forwarded without creating unicast reachability to the source.

Route Targets decide what each VRF imports and exports. A VPN-S VRF that holds extranet sources can be given an export Route Target for the extranet routes, and the VPN-R VRFs that hold the receivers can be given the same target as an import target. Arbitrarily complex policies can be built this way. Unicast routes also have to be distributed: a VRF that holds a source but not the group's Rendezvous Point must import a unicast route matching that Rendezvous Point, and a VRF that holds the Rendezvous Point must import a unicast route matching the first-hop designated router of the source.

One constraint matters for everything that follows. If the same address means one system in VPN-A and a different system in VPN-B, then the routes exported for that address from the two VPNs must not have any Route Target in common, or the receiving VRF cannot tell the two systems apart.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver VPN has to import a route that points to the source address, and Route Targets decide what each VPN shares. If two VPNs use the same address for different machines, their routes must not share a Route Target, or the receiver cannot tell the machines apart.

sections.title: Avoiding Misdelivery on a P-Tunnel
sections.content:
Two VPNs may use overlapping address spaces, and inside an extranet the same address can then mean different systems to different members. The RFC works through two cases. In the first, a provider edge router sends an extranet flow and an ordinary flow over the same P-tunnel, and a receiver that joined both tunnels receives the same group from two sources. In the second, one router sends two different extranet flows over the same P-tunnel. In both cases the receiver cannot tell the two copies apart, so the data stream would be corrupted if it forwarded both.

There are two ways out. The first is to check the tunnel: each provider edge router determines the expected P-tunnel for a flow and discards packets that arrive on any other tunnel. The second is to remove the ambiguity by provisioning. The single C-source per (C-S,C-G) or (C-S,C-*) P-tunnel policy keeps one source on each selective tunnel, and the single C-group per (C-*,C-G) P-tunnel policy keeps one group on each such tunnel. If the tunnel checks cannot be applied everywhere, these policies are required, and the VRFs holding extranet sources must also avoid advertising P-tunnels in I-PMSI routes and in (C-*,C-*) S-PMSI routes, because no policy can separate the sources on those tunnels.
sections.plainLanguage: When two VPNs use the same address for different machines, a receiver can get two different copies of the same group and cannot tell them apart. The fix is either to check which tunnel a packet arrived on and drop the wrong one, or to configure the tunnels so that each carries only one source or one group.

sections.title: The Two New Extended Communities
sections.content:
The RFC defines two new BGP Transitive Opaque Extended Communities, and both carry a value field of zero. The Extranet Source Extended Community lets a customer edge router mark a route as an extranet route, so that the provider applies the extranet distribution rules to it. A provider edge router that understands the community must ignore the value field, and route reflectors and border routers must pass the community along unchanged. A customer edge router should not attach it to a route whose Route Targets are set by some other means.

The Extranet Separation Extended Community marks routes that belong to the extranet side of a separated VRF. It is set to zero on origination, ignored on reception, and passed unchanged by intermediate routers. The UMH-eligible routes and the A-D routes exported from a VRF that uses extranet separation carry it, so that a receiver can tell an extranet tunnel from an ordinary one.
sections.plainLanguage: Two new BGP markers are defined. One says that a route belongs to an extranet source, and the other says that a route belongs to the extranet side of a separated VPN. Both carry no data, only a flag.

sections.title: Finding the Expected P-Tunnel
sections.content:
When BGP is the provider-to-provider control protocol, a receiver VRF works out which tunnel a flow should arrive on. It first finds the upstream provider edge router, then looks at the auto-discovery routes that router originated and checks whether one of them matches the flow. The RFC adds extranet conditions to that check. A selective route for one source and group only matches when the single-source policy is in place, or when the selected UMH route for that source shares a Route Target with the auto-discovery route and one of the shared targets is an import target of the VRF. A route with a wildcard group needs the single-group policy or a matching set of targets, and a route with both wildcards needs matching targets and either both sides or neither side carrying the extranet separation community.

When PIM is the control protocol, the receiver side is set up with Incoming Extranet RTs and the source side with Outgoing Extranet RTs, and a VRF that holds both sources and receivers needs both kinds. Each VRF with receivers originates one I-PMSI auto-discovery route per incoming extranet target, each with its own RD, and the provider treats the tunnels carrying a given extranet target as one emulated LAN.
sections.plainLanguage: A receiving router works out which tunnel the flow should arrive on, and drops the flow if it turns up on a different one. With BGP the check uses shared Route Targets; with PIM the two VPNs are wired together with extra Route Targets for the extranet.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 6513 and RFC 6514 apply. Misconfigured Route Targets can cause a VPN security violation, in which a packet is delivered to a VPN that policy says it should not reach, and so can a manual list of extranet sources that is wrong. The procedures of this RFC do not encrypt or protect the data crossing the provider backbone, so they do not by themselves give privacy or integrity against an attack on that network.

Overlapping address spaces are the main risk. When a VPN-R receiver takes an extranet flow from a VPN-S source, the source address is imported into the VPN-R VRF. If that address is also the address of a VPN-R source that is not an extranet source, the receiver may get the wrong flow. The RFC requires that the addresses of extranet sources and receivers are not taken from the overlapping part of the address space, and that any route imported into a VRF matches only addresses that are unambiguous in that VRF.

The RFC also warns that a source sending both extranet and ordinary flows lets any receiver of the extranet flow receive the ordinary flow too, and that the service provider cannot control which flows a source sends. Providers must make this clear to the customers who run the sources.
sections.plainLanguage: Misconfiguration can deliver traffic to a VPN that should not receive it, and the rules here do not encrypt the data crossing the provider network. The biggest risk is two VPNs using the same address for different machines, which the provisioning has to avoid.

items.title: Expected P-tunnel check
items.text: The receiving router discards packets that arrive on another tunnel.

items.title: Single C-source per tunnel
items.text: Each selective tunnel carries flows from one source only.

items.title: Single C-group per tunnel
items.text: Each tunnel with a wildcard group carries one group only.

items.title: No shared inclusive tunnels
items.text: Inclusive and all-wildcard tunnels are avoided where they would mix sources.
